title: Can Life Keep Up When the Planet Changes Too Fast? Scientists Have a New Answer
summary: Imagine you're in a race, but the finish line keeps moving faster and faster. That's what it's like for animals when the environment changes too quickly. Scientists at MIT and the University of Leicester wondered: can this idea explain why huge numbers of species sometimes go extinct all at once? They built a math model to test it. Think of a bell-shaped curve: most animals adapt at a medium speed, but only a few can adapt super fast or super slow. When the environment shifts too quickly, the slowpokes can't keep up, and they disappear. The team checked their model against 27 big environmental changes over the last 450 million years. They looked at how fast the carbon cycle changed—a clue about the climate—and compared it to how many animal groups died out. The model worked! It correctly predicted the severity of almost every mass extinction. So, the next time you hear about climate change, remember: it's not just about warmer weather. It's about whether life can sprint fast enough to survive.
why_it_matters: Understanding how fast change can cause extinctions helps you see why slowing down climate change is important to protect animals we love, like polar bears and butterflies, and even our own future.

background_read: Earth's history includes several mass extinctions, such as the one that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
Researchers from MIT (a leading U.S. science university) and the University of Leicester investigated whether a too-fast changing environment is to blame.
They looked at the carbon cycle — how carbon moves between the air, oceans, and living things — as a clue to past climate speed.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists from MIT and the University of Leicester
WHAT: A mathematical model showing that when the environment changes too quickly, slow-adapting species go extinct, leading to mass extinctions
WHERE: Studied data from 27 past events across the globe, covering 450 million years
WHY: To explain past extinctions and warn that today's rapid climate change could be just as dangerous

perspectives.description: The model could help scientists identify which animals need the most help to survive a warming planet.
Some might argue that if extinctions are natural, we don't need to change our behavior, but scientists say today's changes are human-caused and unusually fast.
The bell-curve idea shows that most species adapt at a medium pace, so when the climate outpaces that, many can't keep up — a simple but powerful warning.
